strengths: Presents a clear and practical scale-wise distillation framework (SwD) that combines progressive spatial resolution with few-step diffusion distillation and can be integrated with distribution-matching methods such as DMD2.
The latent spectral analysis provides useful intuition for why high-noise diffusion steps may be modeled at lower resolutions, motivating the approach.
Introduces patch distribution matching (PDM), a simple model-free loss that is shown to substantially improve performance and can even serve as a standalone distillation objective.
Conducts large-scale experiments on SD3.5 Medium/Large, with automated metrics, human preference studies, and comparisons to several strong baselines (e.g., DMD2, SDXL-Turbo, Switti, Infinity).
Reports consistent ~2x reductions in generation and training time, and human evaluation suggests gains in image complexity and competitiveness on aesthetics/text relevance.
Ablations cover important design choices, including time schedule shifting, scale-wise training, synthetic data, and PDM, providing insight into the method.
weaknesses: The paper overclaims quality preservation: FID is often substantially worse than full-scale variants and baselines (e.g., COCO FID 23.0 vs. 20.4 for full-scale 6-step; MJHQ FID 13.6 vs. 13.4), contradicting statements of 'no noticeable quality degradation' and 'significantly outperforms counterparts.'

A closely related method, Pagoda (progressive growing of a one-step generator from a low-resolution diffusion teacher), is cited but not discussed or compared experimentally, weakening the novelty and positioning of SwD.

The PDM objective with the linear kernel essentially matches mean spatial token features, making its technical novelty limited; the paper lacks deeper analysis of why patch distribution matching is preferable over standard feature-matching/MMD variants beyond a simple naive baseline.
The scale and timestep schedules are manually chosen and not adaptive; the spectral analysis is only qualitative and does not formally guarantee safe downsampling or information preservation.

Important implementation/reproducibility details are missing or under-specified, such as handling variable resolution positional embeddings in DiT/SD3.5, PDM kernel bandwidth for RBF, exact time-shift procedure, and statistical significance of human evaluation.

The evaluation is mixed: FID is much worse than several baselines, and human evaluation is reported only as aggregate bars without confidence intervals or significance tests, so the central claim of outperforming counterparts under equal budget is not fully established.

strengths: Presents a timely and practically relevant direction: combining scale-wise generation with diffusion distillation to reduce inference and training cost.
The spectral analysis of latent diffusion models is a reasonable motivation and connects to prior observations about coarse-to-fine diffusion generation.
The proposed SwD method is clearly described and integrates naturally with DMD2, making it easy to implement on top of an existing distillation pipeline.
The PDM loss is computationally lightweight and does not require an additional discriminator or fake diffusion model, which is attractive from an efficiency standpoint.
The paper evaluates on large-scale text-to-image models (SD3.5 Medium/Large), reports multiple automated metrics, and includes human preference studies.
Ablations cover several important design choices, including time shifting, scale schedule, scale-wise training, synthetic vs. real data, and PDM variants.
The method achieves meaningful speedups in both generation and training in some settings, e.g., roughly 2x compared with full-scale counterparts.
The writing is generally readable, and the related work section covers several relevant areas such as diffusion distillation, scale-wise generation, and dynamic inference.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Progressive or scale-wise generation has been explored in cascaded diffusion models, progressive-growing GANs/VAEs, and related work such as Pagoda [31]. The paper does not adequately differentiate SwD from these approaches or compare against the closest progressive-distillation baseline.

The central claim that scale-wise generation suffers 'without loss in performance' is not supported by the reported metrics. In Table 2, scale-wise 6-step FID is 23.0 on COCO vs. 20.4 for full-scale 6-step, and scale-wise 4-step FID is 23.3 vs. 20.3 for full-scale 2-step. FID is consistently worse, yet the abstract claims significant outperformance and no loss.

The evaluation is not fully convincing. The main comparison in Table 4 shows SwD/M has much worse FID than DMD2-SDXL (23.0 vs. 14.3 on COCO; 13.6 vs. 7.2 on MJHQ), despite similar latency. The paper emphasizes IR/PickScore/GenEval but does not reconcile the major FID gap.

The human evaluation is under-specified and lacks statistical rigor. It is unclear how many assessors participated, how many comparisons were made, whether confidence intervals or significance tests were computed, and how the contradictory FID vs. human-preference results should be interpreted.

The theoretical motivation is weak. The spectral analysis is qualitative and only covers two VAEs; it does not formally establish when lower-resolution modeling is safe, how aliasing is avoided, or how much high-frequency information is lost. The claim that high frequencies are 'masked' does not imply that discarding them incurs no cost.

The PDM loss is mischaracterized. Equation (2) with a linear kernel matches the per-image mean of spatial tokens, not a true patch distribution or MMD over patch distributions. It is essentially feature-mean matching rather than a general distribution-matching objective, and the theoretical justification is thin.

Baseline comparisons are not fully controlled. Different models use different backbones, parameter counts, training data, and optimization budgets, making claims of 'state-of-the-art' performance difficult to support. The paper also lacks a direct comparison to DMD2 trained on SD3.5, Pagoda, or other progressive-distillation methods.

The paper does not sufficiently analyze the trade-off between resolution reduction and sample quality. Scale-wise inference is faster partly because it operates at lower resolution, but the quality degradation in FID and human aesthetics/complexity is downplayed.

Reproducibility is limited. No code or model release is mentioned, variance across runs is not reported, and key choices such as the time schedule shifting rule and scale schedule selection are heuristic without sensitivity analysis.

The positioning overstates the contribution relative to prior work on cascaded diffusion, progressive generation, and dynamic token/resolution diffusion. The paper would benefit from clearer novelty claims and stronger empirical evidence before being competitive at a top-tier venue.
Broader impact and ethical considerations for large-scale text-to-image generation are not discussed, which is a minor but notable omission for a high-impact generative modeling paper.

strengths: Introduces a novel scale-wise distillation framework (SwD) that combines next-scale prediction with diffusion distillation, an underexplored direction for few-step generation.
Provides a useful spectral analysis of VAE latents in SDXL and SD3.5 that motivates operating at lower resolutions for high-noise timesteps, grounding the method in an empirical observation.
Proposes Patch Distribution Matching (PDM), a simple and architecture-compatible distribution matching loss that requires no additional trainable networks and improves the main method in ablations.
Demonstrates strong practical benefits: 2x generation/training speedup over full-scale distillation and 2.5x-10x speedup over the teacher while maintaining competitive quality.
Conducts extensive experiments on SD3.5 Medium and Large, including automated metrics, GenEval, latency measurements, and a human preference study.
Ablations are thorough and cover key design choices: time schedule shifting, scale schedule, scale-wise training, synthetic vs. real data, and PDM variants.
The paper is clearly written and well-structured, with helpful figures illustrating the training and sampling procedures.
weaknesses: FID is notably worse than DMD2-SDXL and full-scale DMD2+PDM on COCO and MJHQ, which is not fully explained; the paper emphasizes PS/IR/GenEval but the FID gap is a concern for image fidelity.
The spectral motivation is largely heuristic: it shows that high frequencies are masked by noise but does not rigorously prove that lower-resolution modeling is lossless at the selected timesteps.
The scale and time schedules are manually specified, and there is no adaptive or dynamic schedule, which limits the generality of the approach.

PDM with a linear kernel essentially matches first-order feature statistics; its novelty is moderate, and the claim that it works as a standalone distillation objective is not strongly supported by comparisons to other standalone losses.
The stated dual-purpose claim that scale-wise models serve as image upscalers is not directly evaluated with a dedicated upscaling benchmark or task.
Several highly relevant scale-wise or progressive distillation methods, such as PAGODA, are not empirically compared, so the positioning relative to prior progressive approaches could be stronger.

Human evaluation is shown mostly as bar charts without detailed win rates or significance tests in the main text; the slight degradation in defects against DMD2-SDXL remains a potential quality concern.
Reproducibility could be improved: there is no mention of released code/weights, and training requires 8 A100 GPUs with synthetic data generation details delegated to the appendix.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated scale-wise distillation framework that combines progressive resolution generation with few-step distribution matching, enabling lower-resolution computation at high noise levels.
Provides latent-space spectral analysis for image and video diffusion models, supporting the core design intuition across both spatial and temporal dimensions.

Proposes a simple and effective MMD-based distillation loss using pretrained diffusion model features, requiring no additional trainable model and working both standalone and alongside DMD/GAN objectives.
Extensive experiments across state-of-the-art text-to-image and text-to-video models (SDXL, SD3.5, FLUX, Wan2.1) with automatic metrics, runtime comparisons, and human preference studies.

Demonstrates meaningful practical gains, including roughly 2x speedup for text-to-image and 3x for text-to-video, with quality competitive with or better than teacher/few-step baselines in several settings.
Provides substantial implementation details, schedules, runtime measurement setup, and human evaluation protocol, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core scale-wise/progressive generation idea is incremental relative to prior cascaded, relay, pyramidal, and multi-stage diffusion approaches; the main novelty lies in combining it with few-step distillation and the MMD objective.

The proposed MMD loss is ultimately simplified to a squared distance between per-image mean spatial features, which is closer to feature mean matching than a full distributional MMD; theoretical justification for per-image averaging and the linear kernel is limited.

Evaluation results are mixed: FID is often worse than strong baselines (e.g., FLUX-SwD 26.4 vs. FLUX-Schnell 16.5; SDXL-SwD 21.3 vs. DMD2 14.1), and human preference studies use a relatively limited set of 128 prompts with some noted defect degradation.
The claimed seamless integration with existing distillation methods is not universal: DMD degrades performance for SDXL and Wan2.1, forcing reliance on MMD-only training in those cases.
Scale and timestep schedules remain important hyperparameters, with limited sensitivity analysis beyond constant-schedule comparisons, which may complicate adoption.

strengths: Introduces SwD, a scale-wise few-step distillation framework that combines progressive generation with distribution matching and demonstrates practical speedups for large text-to-image and text-to-video diffusion models.
Provides a simple MMD-based distillation objective that can be used as a standalone loss and is computationally efficient, with useful ablations on kernel choice, noising, and feature averaging.
Conducts a broad empirical study across SDXL, SD3.5, FLUX, and Wan2.1, including automatic metrics, human preference evaluation, runtime measurements, and training-time comparisons.
Reports substantial efficiency gains: roughly 2x speedup for text-to-image and 3x for text-to-video under comparable settings, with training speedups as well.
Motivates the method with latent-space spectral analysis and extends it to video temporal frequencies, offering some empirical insight into coarse-to-fine diffusion behavior.
Includes practical ablations on noisy latent upsampling strategies, scale schedules, and full-resolution versus scale-wise generation.
weaknesses: The proposed MMD objective is ultimately reduced to a per-image MSE between mean-pooled teacher features; with the linear kernel, it does not match patch-level token distributions and is essentially feature matching, so the 'patch-level MMD' framing overstates the methodological novelty.

The spectral analysis motivates lower-resolution sampling, but the actual training downscales in pixel space before VAE encoding rather than operating on lower-resolution latent samples; the scale and timestep schedules remain hand-tuned hyperparameters, so the analysis does not directly validate the training procedure.

Evaluation is mixed: FID degrades substantially for several models against baselines or teachers (e.g., SDXL-SwD, FLUX-SwD, SD3.5-L-SwD), while gains are mainly on preference metrics; the claim that SwD 'largely outperforms alternatives' is not uniformly supported across metrics.

DMD is reported to be ineffective for SDXL and Wan2.1, so integration with existing distribution matching methods is not as seamless as claimed, and MMD-only models show more defects in human evaluation.

Baselines are heterogeneous and trained with different data and compute budgets; some comparisons may not cleanly isolate the effect of scale-wise distillation, and automatic metrics lack error bars or confidence intervals.

Key architectural details are missing, such as how the model handles changing resolutions (e.g., positional embedding interpolation, scale conditioning) and how a single generator is trained across scales, which limits reproducibility.
The human study is limited (128 prompts, 3 responses per comparison) and lacks statistical significance analysis, making it insufficient to fully establish quality parity or superiority.

Runtime measurements replace the original VAEs with TinyVAEs for all models; it is unclear whether quality metrics use the same VAEs and whether this choice affects fairness or the reported speed-quality trade-off.
Comparisons to other progressive or multi-scale diffusion methods (e.g., Pyramidal Flow Matching, Relay Diffusion) are mostly discussed in related work rather than empirically evaluated.

strengths: Presents a novel and well-motivated scale-wise distillation framework (SwD) that progressively increases spatial and temporal latent resolution within a single few-step generator, addressing an underexplored efficiency axis beyond step reduction.

The spectral analysis of latent spaces, including video temporal frequencies, provides useful empirical grounding for the method and strengthens the motivation for lower-resolution modeling at high noise levels.

Introduces a simple yet effective patch-level MMD distillation objective that is easy to implement, requires no additional trainable model, and improves convergence when combined with existing distillation losses; ablation studies show its individual effectiveness.

Extensive empirical evaluation spans multiple large-scale text-to-image and text-to-video models (SDXL, SD3.5-M/L, FLUX, Wan2.1) with comparisons to strong baselines, automatic metrics, and professional human preference studies.
Demonstrates substantial practical speedups (~2x for T2I, ~3x for T2V) and largely competitive or better quality relative to teachers and few-step alternatives under similar compute budgets.
Provides detailed implementation information, schedules, hyperparameters, latency measurements, and appendix analyses on upscaling strategies and scale schedules, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The scale-wise schedules and timestep adjustments remain hand-tuned hyperparameters; the spectral analysis offers intuition but no formal guarantee of information preservation or an automated way to select schedules.

The strongest results rely on the full objective combining MMD with DMD and GAN losses, which still require extra trainable models; the MMD-only variant is competitive but weaker and exhibits more defects, so the claimed self-contained/lightweight advantage is only partially realized.

Some automatic metrics, especially FID, are worse than baselines or teachers for several SwD models, and the human study shows only comparable text relevance and occasional defects, so the quality claims are not uniformly supported across metrics.

Generalization depends on the teacher's low-resolution generation ability: for SDXL and Wan2.1, DMD degrades performance and is replaced by MMD-only training, raising questions about robustness across base models and loss combinations.

The MMD objective is closely related to feature matching and prior MMD-based distillation work (e.g., IMM), and the paper does not provide theoretical analysis of why the linear-kernel per-image token mean matching is particularly effective.
Text-to-video evaluation is limited to a single 1.3B model, and VBench-2.0 overall gains over CausVid are modest, leaving broader validation on larger video diffusion models uncertain.
